summary: The most common apple disease. A fungus causes velvety olive spots on leaves and dark scabs on fruit; severe attacks drop leaves early and weaken the tree.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety leaf spots with feathery edges that later turn black
Twisted or puckered young leaves; early leaf drop in bad years
Brown, raised, corky scabs on fruit, which may crack
key_sign: Velvety olive-to-black spots with blurred, feathery edges.
favourable_conditions: Cool, wet spring weather; infection needs several hours of leaf wetness.
spread: Spores overwinter in fallen infected leaves and are splashed or blown onto new leaves in spring.

today: Pick off badly spotted leaves you can reach and remove them from the orchard
Note which trees are affected so you can monitor them
this_week: If fruit quality matters, apply a protectant fungicide registered for apple scab, especially before forecast rain
Prune crowded branches to let air and sunlight dry the canopy
next_two_weeks: Repeat protection at the label interval while wet weather continues
Check new leaves and young fruit for fresh spots

chemical: Protectant fungicides containing captan or mancozeb, applied before infection periods
Systemic options such as myclobutanil or other DMI fungicides; rotate groups to avoid resistance
organic: Sulfur or lime-sulfur sprays, applied before rain
Copper sprays at green tip only (can scar fruit later)
cultural: Rake and destroy or compost fallen leaves in autumn to remove the overwintering source
Prune for an open canopy; avoid overhead irrigation

prevention: Plant scab-resistant or immune varieties (for example Liberty, Freedom, Pixie Crunch)
Remove nearby susceptible ornamental crabapples, which can carry the disease

summary: A fungus that causes 'frog-eye' leaf spots, branch cankers and a firm black rot of fruit. Most common on stressed or injured trees.
symptoms: Round leaf spots with a purple border and tan centre (frog-eye spots)
Fruit rot with brown and black rings; fruit dries into black mummies
key_sign: Round spots with a purple border and a tan centre.
favourable_conditions: Warm, wet weather; trees weakened by winter injury, fire blight or poor care.
spread: Survives in dead wood, cankers and mummified fruit; spores spread by rain splash.

today: Remove mummified fruit from the tree and the ground
Mark branches with cankers for pruning
this_week: Prune out dead wood and cankers at least 15 cm below visible damage in dry weather; disinfect tools between cuts
If many leaves are spotted, apply a fungicide registered for black rot on apple
next_two_weeks: Destroy all prunings (do not leave them in the orchard)
Reduce tree stress: water in dry spells and fertilise according to a soil test

chemical: Captan and other fungicides labelled for apple black rot, usually combined with the scab programme
organic: Strict sanitation is the main tool; sulfur offers limited protection
cultural: Remove cankers, dead branches and mummies, which are the main sources of spores
Control fire blight and avoid wounds, which open the door to infection

prevention: Keep trees vigorous and free of dead wood
Clean up fallen fruit every season

summary: A rust fungus that needs both apple and juniper (red cedar) to complete its life cycle. Causes bright orange leaf spots; rarely serious on resistant varieties.
symptoms: Yellow spots that turn bright orange with a red border on the upper leaf
Small tube-like structures on the underside of older spots
Orange, slightly raised spots on fruit
key_sign: Bright orange spots, often with a red border.
favourable_conditions: Wet spring weather when junipers nearby release spores from orange, jelly-like galls.
spread: Spores blow from galls on juniper or red cedar trees to apple leaves; it does not spread apple to apple.

today: Look for brown galls or orange jelly-like growths on nearby juniper or cedar trees
this_week: Remove galls from nearby junipers where practical
On susceptible varieties with heavy infection, apply a fungicide registered for rust
next_two_weeks: Monitor new leaves; most infection happens from pink bud to a few weeks after petal fall

chemical: Myclobutanil or other DMI fungicides labelled for rust, applied from pink bud through early fruit set
organic: Sulfur sprays give partial protection when applied before infection
cultural: Remove nearby junipers or their galls to break the cycle

prevention: Avoid planting apples close to eastern red cedar

summary: No disease signs were found on this apple leaf.
key_sign: Uniform green leaf with no spots.

this_week: Check a few leaves on each tree, including the undersides
next_two_weeks: Keep monitoring, especially after rainy periods in spring

cultural: Keep the canopy open and clean up fallen leaves

prevention: Remove fallen leaves and fruit in autumn
